nameStory: The smooth flounder gets its name from its notably smooth skin, which lacks the rough scales or spines found on many other flatfish. Unlike some of its bumpy relatives, this flounder feels surprisingly soft and slippery to the touch, making 'smooth' the perfect descriptor for this sleek bottom-dweller.
description: The smooth flounder is a fascinating flatfish that lives its adult life lying sideways on sandy or muddy bottoms. Like all flounders, it starts life swimming upright like a normal fish, but as it grows, one eye migrates to join the other on what becomes the 'top' side of its flattened body. This remarkable fish can grow up to 12 inches long and has mastered the art of camouflage, changing colors to blend perfectly with the seafloor.

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Extremely flattened oval body that feels like a soft, flexible pancake when handled - much thinner than any round fish you might catch

idTips.label: Skin Texture
idTips.description: Remarkably smooth, slippery skin without the rough scales or prickly spines of other flatfish - feels almost rubbery to the touch

idTips.label: Eye Position
idTips.description: Both eyes located on the same side of the head (the 'top' side when lying on bottom), giving it a distinctly lopsided appearance

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Variable brown to gray coloration on the eye-side that can change to match surroundings, with a pale white underside that never sees sunlight

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Typically 6-12 inches long, fitting comfortably in two hands when caught

idTips.label: Habitat
idTips.description: Found lying motionless on soft sandy or muddy bottoms in shallow coastal waters, often partially buried with just eyes showing

habitat: Smooth flounders inhabit shallow coastal waters throughout New England, from tide pools to depths of about 90 feet. They prefer soft, sandy or muddy bottoms where they can easily bury themselves, and are commonly found in salt marshes, estuaries, and protected bays where fresh and salt water mix. Look for them in areas with gentle currents where small invertebrates they feed on are abundant.

seasonality.spring: Smooth flounders become more active as waters warm, moving into shallower areas to feed and spawn. This is when they're most likely to be spotted by tide pool explorers.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity season when flounders are most abundant in shallow waters and easiest to observe. Their color-changing abilities are most dramatic during warm weather feeding.
seasonality.fall: Fish begin moving to slightly deeper waters but remain active feeders. Still commonly encountered by anglers and beachcombers before winter sets in.
seasonality.winter: Flounders move to deeper waters and become less active, making them harder to find in typical shallow-water exploring spots.

funFact: Baby smooth flounders start life swimming upright like regular fish with eyes on both sides of their head, but as they grow, their left eye literally travels across the top of their skull to join the right eye - it's like nature's own magic trick happening in slow motion over several weeks!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with winter flounder, but the smooth flounder's notably slippery, scale-free skin is the giveaway - if it feels rough or sandpapery, it's probably a winter flounder. Remember: smooth flounder = smooth skin!
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'smooth flounder,' this fish is actually in a different genus (Liopsetta) than the common flounder (Pseudopleuronectes), showing how common names can sometimes be misleading about actual relationships between species.
compareHints: The smooth flounder is the only member of its genus (Liopsetta) in New England waters, making it unique among local flatfish. Compared to other righteye flounders like winter flounder, it's distinguished by its exceptionally smooth skin texture and slightly smaller maximum size. While winter flounders feel rough and sandpapery, the smooth flounder lives up to its name with skin that feels almost rubbery.
